title: How to Read the Book of Proverbs Rightly
subtitle: A pastor's guide to interpreting biblical wisdom literature, why a proverb is not a promise, how Hebrew poetry works, and how to apply the book of Proverbs without turning it into a law of guaranteed outcomes

sections.title: The Verse That Broke Someone
sections.body:
Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it. I have watched that verse break a faithful mother. She did everything. She prayed over the crib, taught the catechism, drove to youth group, modeled a quiet and steady faith. And her son walked away anyway, into a far country, and stayed there.

She came to me convinced she had failed God. Because the verse promised her an outcome, and the outcome did not come.

It did not promise her that. Not the way she read it. We had taken a proverb and made it a contract, and then we billed God for breach. This is the most common abuse of the wisest book in the Bible, and it does enormous quiet damage in the pews. Proverbs is not a book of promises with God's signature on the bottom. It is a book of wisdom, and wisdom and promise are not the same thing. Until you know the difference, you will read this book and either despair or grow proud, and both are wrong.

sections.title: What a Proverb Actually Is
sections.body:
A proverb is a short, sharp observation about how life usually goes. It is true the way a road map is true, not the way a guarantee is true. It tells you the way the world generally runs under the ordinary providence of God, so that a son or daughter learning to live can move with the grain of reality rather than against it.

A proverb states the rule. It does not cover every exception. That is not a flaw. That is what a proverb is.

The lazy hand grows poor, and the diligent grow rich. Generally. Tell that to Joseph in the pit or Job on the ash heap. The proverb is still true as a rule, and the righteous sufferer is still real, and both belong in the same Bible. Job and Proverbs sit a few books apart for a reason. One gives the rule. The other guards the rule from becoming a club used to beat the suffering. Read a proverb as a wise generalization and it will guide you. Read it as an ironclad law and it will lie to you the first time life does not cooperate.

sections.title: The Shape of Hebrew Wisdom
sections.body:
Proverbs is poetry, and Hebrew poetry does its work in pairs. A line says something, and the next line answers it, sharpening or completing or contrasting the first. This is parallelism, and it is the engine of the book. The wise are contrasted with the fool. The path of life is set against the path of death. You are meant to feel the two roads diverging.

The poetry compresses. It says less so it can land harder. You have to slow down and let both lines speak.

And the images are concrete because wisdom is concrete. An ant. A nagging wife in the corner of a roof. A man who hugs a lazy bed. A word fitly spoken, like apples of gold in settings of silver. The book teaches you to see God's order woven into ordinary things, into your money and your mouth and your marriage bed. Do not flatten the poetry into prose maxims. Read it slowly, picture by picture, and let the pictures preach. The form is not decoration. The form is the meaning.

sections.title: The Fear at the Door
sections.body:
The book hands you its master key in the seventh verse. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. That is the doorway, and you cannot read the rest rightly until you have walked through it. All the practical counsel, the budgeting and the tongue and the friendships, hangs on one prior reality. There is a God, and you are not him, and wisdom starts the moment you bow.

This is what separates biblical wisdom from a self help book. It is not a set of tips for a better life. It is the fear of God, worked out in the kitchen and the office.

Miss this and Proverbs becomes a pile of clever sayings you could find on any calendar. Keep this and the whole book becomes worship. The reason you guard your tongue is that God hears it. The reason you work hard and give freely is that the world belongs to him. Strip the fear of the LORD out of Proverbs and you have moralism. Leave it in, and you have a life bent toward God in every small decision. Everything else in the book is commentary on that first line.

sections.title: Where the Wisdom Was Heading
sections.body:
In the eighth chapter, wisdom stops being a topic and starts being a voice. She speaks. She was there at the beginning, beside God as he laid the foundations of the world, rejoicing before him. The book is reaching for something larger than good advice. It is reaching for a person.

The New Testament tells you who. Christ is the wisdom of God. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

This is why a Christian cannot read Proverbs as mere self improvement. The book that begins with the fear of the LORD ends, in the fullness of time, at the feet of the one who is wiser than Solomon. Every call to choose the right path is finally a call to follow him who is the way. You have not read Proverbs to the bottom until you have heard it point past itself to Christ, who kept the wisdom we squander and became wisdom for us. Read it there, and the budgeting and the tongue and the friendships all find their center.

sections.title: Wisdom for People Who Will Get It Wrong
sections.body:
So read Proverbs often, and read it as what it is. A book of wise generalizations, not signed guarantees. Poetry, not prose. The fear of the LORD, not life hacks. A finger pointing at Christ, not a self help shelf.

And read it humbly, because the book itself says the wise man keeps learning and only the fool thinks he has arrived.

I have preached this book and then gone home and used my tongue like a fool. The distance between knowing the proverb and living it is the whole of the Christian life. That is why we need it written down, and read again, and prayed over. Proverbs will not promise you that your children come home or your investments pay off. It will do something better. It will teach you the fear of God, and bend your ordinary days toward him, and send you to the one who is wisdom himself. Take it as wisdom. Do not take it as a contract. And go live.
